# Buildings (BIM)

A building is a shape program whose parts are its building elements. The building vocabulary (`crates/plugins/shape/src/bim.js`, loaded after the prelude) makes the geometry and says what each part is: IFC class, level, property sets (`Pset_WallCommon`…), base quantities (`Qto_…`: lengths mm, areas m², volumes m³), type, tag, classification. Read `bim.js` before writing one; `examples/house` is a worked two-storey house.

- Structure: `site({ name, latitude, longitude, elevation (m), address, north })`, `building({ name, address })`, `const L1 = level("First floor", 3000, { height: 2800 })` (elevation is project z of the floor; elements take `level: L1`). `grid("Grid", { x: [0, 4500, 9000], y: [0, 3500], level })` draws numbered/lettered lines with bubbles and returns `{ at(i, j) }`.
- Elements (each returns a list of parts; spread them into what the program returns): `wall(name, { from, to, thickness, height, level, base, align: center|left|right, external, loadBearing, openings, profile: [[along, up]…] (a gable's elevation), extend })`; `walls(name, { points, closed, names, openings: [[…], …] per segment })` mitres the corners; `slab(name, { outline: points|Profile, thickness, level (its top), holes, kind: FLOOR|ROOF|BASESLAB|LANDING })`; `roof(name, { x, y, width, depth, kind: gable|hip|shed|flat, slope, thickness, overhang, ridge: x|y, level (the eaves) })`; `column(name, { at, size|diameter|section, height, level })`; `beam(name, { from, to (top of beam, 3D), size|section })` with `section("IPE 300" | "HEA 160" | "HEB 200" | "SHS 100x5" | "RHS 120x80x5" | "CHS 114.3x5" | "200x400")`; `stair(name, { at (foot, centre of width), dir (degrees), width, rise, going, maxRiser, waist, level })` (equal risers, plan treads dashed above the cut, arrow up); `ramp(name, { at, dir, length, width, rise })`; `railing(name, { path, height, spacing, bars })`; `curtainWall(name, { from, to, height, panel: [w, h], mullion: [w, d] })` (mullions and panels in one IfcCurtainWall); `rebar(name, { path: [[x,y,z]…], diameter, count, spacing, direction, mark, grade, embedded: "Ground slab" })` (bending schedule quantities: diameter, length each, count, total, kg; `embedded` names the slab, beam or wall the bars are cast in — always give it, or every interference check reports the bars overlapping their concrete).
- Openings in a wall's `openings`: `door({ at (centre along the wall from its start), preset: single|double|sliding|entrance|garage, width, height, swing: left|right, side: 1|-1 })`, `window({ at, preset: fixed|casement|double|triple|sliding|high, width, height, sill })`, `opening({ at, width, height, sill })`. Each cuts its host, is declared as an opening hosted by the wall and filled by the door or window (one part each, bought: part number = its type), tagged D01, W01… in order, with its plan symbol (swing arc, sill lines). Move a door by changing `at`: the wall is re-cut, the opening follows.
- Rooms are not parts: `space(name, { outline: points (or [outer, hole…]), level, height, longName, usage, zone })`; `zone(name, [space names])`. Any other part: `part(name, solid, { material, ifc: "IfcFurniture" | { class, predefined, type, level, tag, psets, quantities, classification: { system, code, name } } })`. Several parts as one element: `group(name, "IfcStair", { level })` and `ifc: { parent: name }` on each part.
- Untagged parts are exported as IfcBuildingElementProxy; their level is the highest at or below their bottom. Floor instances of a tower with no `level()` anywhere become storeys named after the top-level instances.

Use it:

```
./ise bim [id|project]                                   levels and what stands on each, rooms with areas, zones, grids, untagged parts
./ise schedule [id|project] [--class wall,door] [--level "Ground floor"] [--by level,class] [--csv] [--psets] [--out file.csv]
./ise ifc export [id|project] [file.ifc]                 IFC4 (project › site › building › storeys, elements with geometry, openings, spaces, zones, grids, materials, psets, Qto)
./ise ifc import <file.ifc>                              adds the file as a shape `return importIfc("<sha>")` (elements as parts, with everything above)
./ise plan [id|project] --level "Ground floor" [--cut 1200] [--pdf f.pdf] [--dxf f.dxf]   level plan: walls cut solid, doors with swings, rooms with areas, grid, dimensions, north
./ise plan [id|project] --section x 5000 [--looking east] | --elevation south   [--sheet A3] [--scale 100]
```

Schedules come from the engine (never count by hand): each element's declared quantities plus its measured volume (m³) and, for walls, the openings in it; spaces with floor area, perimeter and volume; zones with their spaces' totals; `--by level,class` totals counts and every additive quantity. The BOM (`./ise bom`) lists each line's IFC class. The person drops an `.ifc` file on the view to import it, and has the building's levels, schedules, IFC export and plans in the Building tab of the workbench (B). Say plainly what IFC import approximated (the import's notes: curved B-rep faces by their edge loops, half-space clips left uncut).
